lessons.title: Reproductive Anatomy and Cycles
lessons.body:
To breed sheep successfully, you must understand the basic parts of the ram and ewe and how their cycles work. The ram's testicles produce sperm and testosterone. A healthy ram has two firm, equal-sized testicles. The penis is inside a sheath and extends during mating. The ewe has two ovaries that release eggs (ova), a uterus where lambs grow, a cervix, and a vagina. The vulva is the external opening. In Africa, most sheep are seasonal breeders, but tropical breeds like the Red Maasai and DjallonkÃ© can breed year-round if feed is good.

The ewe's estrous cycle lasts about 17 days (range 14â19). She is in heat (estrus) for 24â36 hours. During heat, she may stand still when the ram nudges her, wag her tail, and have a swollen, reddish vulva. Ovulation happens 24â30 hours after heat begins. If she is not mated, she returns to heat in about 17 days. Pregnancy (gestation) lasts about 147 days (range 142â152).

Rams are not seasonal like ewes, but their fertility drops in extreme heat. A ram can serve 5â10 ewes in a 17-day cycle. Young rams (under 18 months) should serve fewer ewes. To check if a ewe is pregnant, you can use a ram harness with a crayon: mark the ram's chest with a crayon, and when he mounts a ewe, she gets marked. If she returns to heat, she was not pregnant. Or use ultrasound after 40 days.

Practical signs of heat: ewe stands for the ram, seeks him out, and may bleat more. In hand-mating, bring the ewe to the ram when she shows these signs. Record the date. Count 147 days later for expected lambing. Keep a breeding calendar. In Africa, many farmers use a teaser ram (a vasectomized ram) to detect heat. A teaser ram cannot impregnate but will mount and mark ewes in heat. This helps you plan mating and save feed.

Feed is the biggest factor. Flush ewes (give extra feed) 2â3 weeks before mating to increase ovulation rate. Give 200â300g of maize or sorghum per ewe per day, plus good pasture. For rams, keep them in good body condition (score 3 out of 5) but not fat. Trim their hooves and treat for worms before mating. A healthy ram and well-fed ewes give more lambs.

lessons.title: Selection of Breeding Rams and Ewes
lessons.body:
Choosing the right breeding stock is the cheapest way to improve your flock. Never keep a ram or ewe just because it is available. Select for health, fertility, mothering ability, and growth. In Africa, adapt to local conditions: choose animals that tolerate heat, ticks, and poor feed. Start with your best 20% of ewes and a proven ram.

For a ram: buy or keep a ram that is at least 12â18 months old, with two large, firm testicles. Check for equal size, no lumps, and no signs of disease. His scrotum should be free of wounds. Look at his feet: no foot rot, no long hooves. He should walk easily. His body condition score should be 3â4 (on a 1â5 scale). A ram that is too fat cannot mate well. Check his eyes for anemia (pale inside eyelids means worms). Treat him for internal parasites 3â4 weeks before mating. A good ram has a strong libido: when you put him with a ewe in heat, he should mount quickly. Avoid rams that are aggressive to people or too lazy.

For ewes: select ewes that have lambed before and raised twins. A ewe that produces twins and feeds them well is valuable. Check her udder: two teats, no lumps, no mastitis. She should have a good body condition (score 3). Avoid ewes with bad teeth, chronic lameness, or a history of abortion. Age matters: ewes 2â6 years old are most productive. Replace ewes after 6â7 years. In Africa, keep ewes that shed parasites naturally or need fewer dewormings.

Record keeping is key. Ear tag or notch each animal. Write down: date of birth, sire, dam, number of lambs born, weaning weight. Without records, you cannot improve. Use a simple notebook or a smartphone app. Many African farmers use the 'Flock Record' book. Select rams from twin births, from mothers that lamb easily. Do not keep a ram from a difficult birth or from a ewe that produces singles only.

Finally, avoid inbreeding. Do not use a ram on his own daughters or sisters. Bring in a new ram every 2â3 years. If you cannot buy a new ram, swap rams with a neighbour. Inbreeding causes small, weak lambs and lower fertility. Crossbreeding with local breeds can increase hybrid vigour, but keep pure lines if you want consistent traits. Always quarantine a new ram for 3 weeks before mixing with your flock.

lessons.title: Mating Systems and Timing
lessons.body:
Mating systems determine how many ewes a ram serves and how you manage breeding. The three main systems are hand mating, pasture mating, and artificial insemination (AI). For most African smallholders, hand mating and pasture mating are practical. AI requires trained technicians and liquid nitrogen, so it is less common but available in some areas.

Hand mating: you bring a ewe in heat to a ram for a single service. Use a teaser ram or check ewes twice daily (morning and evening) for heat signs. When a ewe stands for the teaser, move her to the breeding ram. Let the ram serve her once or twice. Record the date. Then return her to the ewe group. This system lets you know exact mating dates, so you can predict lambing. It also saves the ram's energy. A ram can hand-mate 2â3 ewes per day, but give him rest days. Hand mating works well for small flocks (10â50 ewes).

Pasture mating: you run the ram with the ewes for 6â8 weeks. This is less labour but you do not know exact mating dates. Use a ram with a marking harness (crayon on chest) to identify mated ewes. Change crayon colour every 17 days to see returns to heat. A single ram can serve 30â50 ewes in a 6-week period if he is healthy. For 100 ewes, use 2â3 rams. In Africa, pasture mating is common but leads to a spread-out lambing season, which makes management harder.

Timing: ewes cycle every 17 days. If you want lambs at a certain time, plan mating 147 days before. For example, to lamb in the dry season when feed is scarce, avoid mating. Better to mate so lambs are born when grass is plenty. In many African regions, mate in AprilâMay for lambs in SeptemberâOctober (after rains). Or mate in NovemberâDecember for lambs in AprilâMay. Avoid mating in extreme heat (over 35Â°C) because rams become infertile for 6â8 weeks.

Flushing: 2â3 weeks before mating, give ewes extra feed (200â300g grain per day). This increases ovulation and twins. Also, give rams a good diet. During mating, keep rams cool and provide shade and water. Do not overuse a ram: a young ram (12â18 months) should serve no more than 10 ewes in a season. An older ram can serve 30â50. Watch for ram exhaustion: if he lies down often or loses weight, rest him. Rotate rams if possible. Always have a backup ram.

lessons.title: Pregnancy Management
lessons.body:
Once a ewe is mated, pregnancy lasts about 147 days (5 months). Good management during pregnancy ensures healthy lambs and avoids abortion. The first 3 months are early pregnancy: the embryo implants and grows slowly. The last 2 months are rapid growth: 70% of lamb weight is gained then. So feed matters most in the last 6 weeks.

Confirm pregnancy: A ewe that does not return to heat after 17â21 days is likely pregnant. You can also use ultrasound after 40 days (costs $2â5 in many African towns). A ram harness with crayon helps: if she is not marked again, she is probably pregnant. Watch for signs: she may become quieter, her belly grows, and her udder develops in the last month.

Feeding: In early pregnancy, feed normal pasture. In late pregnancy (last 6 weeks), increase energy and protein. Give 300â500g of maize or sorghum per ewe per day, plus good hay or legume hay (e.g., lucerne). Add minerals: a salt lick with calcium and phosphorus. In Africa, many soils lack selenium and copper, so use a mineral supplement. Provide clean water always. Do not feed mouldy hay or spoiled silageâthis causes abortion. Avoid sudden feed changes.

Health care: Deworm ewes 2â3 weeks before lambing, but use a safe dewormer (consult a vet). Vaccinate against clostridial diseases (e.g., pulpy kidney) 4â6 weeks before lambing. This protects the lamb through colostrum. Treat for external parasites (ticks, lice) with a spray or dip. Handle ewes gently: no rough herding, no dog chasing. Stress can cause abortion. Keep ewes away from rams after mating to avoid injury.

Housing: In the last month, move ewes to a clean, dry pen at night. Provide shade and ventilation. Avoid overcrowding. A ewe needs about 1.5â2 square metres. Bed with dry straw. In hot climates, ensure good airflow. In cold areas, protect from wind. Check ewes daily for signs of lambing: restlessness, pawing, separating from flock, swollen vulva, and clear mucus. Have a lambing kit ready: clean towels, iodine, scissors, lubricant, and gloves. If a ewe aborts, isolate her and dispose of the fetus and placenta safely. Abortion can spread disease. Always wash hands after handling aborted material.

lessons.title: Lambing and Assistance
lessons.body:
Lambing is the most critical time. Most ewes lamb without help, but you must be ready. Signs of lambing: the ewe separates from the flock, paws the ground, lies down and gets up, and has a swollen vulva with mucus. She may bleat and look at her flank. First-stage labour lasts 2â6 hours. Second-stage (pushing) should take 30â60 minutes. If she pushes hard for over an hour with no lamb, you must assist.

Prepare a clean lambing pen: 1.5m x 1.5m, dry bedding, fresh water. Wash your hands and arms with soap and water. Put on clean gloves. Use a lubricant (KY jelly or vegetable oil). If the lamb is coming normally, you will see two front feet and a nose. If not, check the position. Common problems: one leg back, head back, or breech (tail first). For a leg back, push the lamb back gently and bring the leg forward. For a head back, push the lamb back and cup the head to bring it forward. For breech, push back and pull the hind legs. Always pull during a contraction, and pull downwards towards the ewe's hocks. Never pull hard. If you cannot correct it in 10 minutes, call a vet or experienced neighbour.

After lambing, clear the lamb's nose and mouth of mucus. If the lamb is not breathing, rub it vigorously with a towel and swing it gently (head down) to clear fluid. Tickle its nose with a straw. If the ewe does not lick the lamb, dry it yourself. Dip the navel in iodine (7% tincture) to prevent infection. Make sure the lamb suckles colostrum within 1 hour. Colostrum is thick, yellow, and rich in antibodies. If the lamb does not suckle, squeeze a little colostrum into its mouth or use a bottle. A lamb needs 200ml of colostrum in the first 6 hours.

Watch for problems: retained placenta (if not passed in 6 hours, call vet), uterine infection (smelly discharge, fever), and mastitis (hot, hard udder). For a ewe that rejects her lamb, restrain her and let the lamb suckle. Sometimes a ewe with twins will reject one. In Africa, many farmers use a 'lambing box' to keep the ewe and lamb together for 1â2 days. Keep records: date, lamb sex, weight, and any assistance given. Good lambing management saves lives.

lessons.title: Neonatal Care
lessons.body:
Neonatal care means caring for the lamb from birth to 2 weeks old. This is when most deaths happen. In Africa, up to 30% of lambs die before weaning, mostly from cold, starvation, and disease. Simple steps can cut that to under 10%.

First, ensure the lamb breathes and is dry. If the ewe does not lick it, rub it with a clean cloth. Put it under a heat lamp or in a warm box if the weather is cold or wet. Lambs cannot regulate body temperature well for the first 2 days. In hot climates, provide shade. In cold, provide dry bedding and windbreaks.

Colostrum is vital. The lamb must drink within the first hour, and at least 200ml in the first 6 hours. Colostrum contains antibodies that protect against disease. If the ewe has no milk or rejects the lamb, use frozen colostrum from another ewe (thaw gently) or a commercial colostrum replacer. You can also milk a healthy ewe and bottle-feed. If the lamb is weak, tube-feed with a stomach tube (ask a vet to show you). Never feed cow's milk in the first dayâit lacks the right antibodies and can cause scours.

After the first day, make sure the lamb suckles every 2â3 hours. A hungry lamb bleats and looks for the udder. Check the ewe's udder for milk. If the ewe has mastitis, treat it and feed the lamb by bottle. Keep the lamb with the ewe in a clean, dry pen for 2â3 days. Then let them join the flock. Ear tag or notch the lamb for identification. Record birth weight (use a hanging scale). A healthy lamb weighs 2â4 kg at birth. Weigh again at 2 weeks to check growth.

Health: Dip the navel in iodine at birth. Watch for joint ill (swollen joints), naval ill (swollen navel), and scours (diarrhoea). Scours can be caused by dirty pens or overfeeding. Treat with electrolytes and consult a vet. Vaccinate lambs at 6â8 weeks against clostridial diseases. Deworm at 4â6 weeks if needed. Provide a creep feed area: a small pen with hay and grain that only lambs can enter. This helps them grow faster. In Africa, many farmers use a 'lamb creep' made of sticks. Always provide clean water. Keep predators away: use a secure night pen. Finally, handle lambs gently to reduce stress. A well-cared lamb will be a productive adult.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Sheep Breeding and Reproduction

Sheep breeding is one of the highest-leverage decisions on an African smallholder or commercial farm. A single ram can influence the genetics of an entire flock for years, and a missed oestrus cycle can cost a producer an entire season of lamb revenue. Yet many farmers treat breeding as a background activity â something that "just happens" â rather than a managed, measurable business process.

This Practical Reference lesson consolidates the core operational knowledge from the Sheep Breeding and Reproduction module into a single working document. It is designed for farm managers, extension officers and agribusiness advisors who need to make fast, evidence-based decisions on: reproductive anatomy and cycles, ram and ewe selection, mating systems and timing, pregnancy management, lambing assistance, and neonatal care â all within African production systems.

The commercial logic is straightforward. A well-managed ewe should produce 1.2â1.8 lambs per year under good conditions, weaned at 3â4 months. If a 50-ewe flock lifts its lambing rate from 80% to 130%, that is an additional 25 lambs per year â at a conservative market value of US$40â80 per weaner in most African markets, that is US$1,000â2,000 in additional gross income from better breeding management alone. The inputs required are knowledge, a record book and disciplined timing, not expensive technology.

1. Reproductive Anatomy and Cycles â What You Must Know Operationally

Ewes are seasonally polyoestrous in many temperate breeds, but most indigenous African breeds (e.g., Red Maasai, DjallonkÃ©, Nguni, Balami, WAD) are either aseasonal or show only mild seasonality, meaning they can breed year-round if nutrition is adequate. This is a major commercial advantage in tropical Africa: it allows producers to target lambing for festive seasons (Eid, Christmas, Easter) when prices peak.

The oestrous cycle in ewes averages 17 days (range 14â19). Oestrus itself lasts 24â36 hours. Ovulation occurs 24â30 hours after the onset of oestrus. The ram's sperm survives 24â48 hours in the ewe's reproductive tract, while the ewe's egg is viable for only 12â18 hours. This narrow window is why mating timing matters commercially: a ram left with ewes continuously will catch most cycles, but hand-mating requires precision.

Puberty in ewe lambs is reached at 6â12 months depending on breed and nutrition, but for business purposes, ewes should not be mated until they reach 60â65% of mature body weight (typically 30â40 kg for indigenous breeds, 45â55 kg for crossbreds). Mating immature ewes produces small lambs, difficult births and stunted dams â a net loss.

2. Selection of Breeding Rams and Ewes

Selection is where genetics meet economics. A ram contributes 50% of the genetics to every lamb in the flock; a ewe contributes 50% to her own lambs. For a 50-ewe flock, one ram is therefore as genetically influential as 25 ewes. This asymmetry means ram selection deserves disproportionate attention.

Key selection criteria for rams: scrotal circumference (â¥30 cm in mature indigenous rams; â¥33 cm in crossbreds), libido (willingness to serve), structural soundness (feet, legs, jaw), body condition score 3.0â3.5, and â critically â proven fertility or a breeding soundness examination. A ram that fails to serve is a silent, expensive failure. In many African markets, a proven ram costs 2â4Ã a cull ram, but the return on that premium is realised within a single lambing season.

For ewes: select for mothering ability, udder soundness (two functional teats), body condition, and previous lambing performance. Ewes that consistently produce twins or triplets under local conditions are genetic gold. Cull ewes that fail to conceive twice, abort repeatedly, or produce weak lambs.

Table 1. Breeding selection targets for African sheep production systems
Trait Ram target Ewe target Why it matters commercially
Body condition score (BCS) 3.0â3.5 (1â5 scale) 2.5â3.5 at mating Thin ewes have lower ovulation rates; fat rams have poor libido
Age at first mating 18 months (proven) 12â18 months (60â65% mature weight) Prevents dystocia and stunted dams
Scrotal circumference â¥30 cm (indigenous), â¥33 cm (crossbred) n/a Correlated with sperm output and fertility
Teat/udder n/a 2 functional teats, no mastitis history Directly affects lamb survival and weaning weight
Previous lambing rate n/a â¥1.3 lambs/ewe/year Identifies high-performing genetics for retention
Health status Vaccinated, dewormed, foot-sound Vaccinated, dewormed, no chronic lameness Reduces abortion and neonatal mortality

Sources: ILRI (2013). Sheep and goat production handbook for Ethiopia; FAO (2012). Phenotypic characterization of animal genetic resources; MLA (2020). Making More From Sheep (adapted for African conditions).

3. Mating Systems and Timing

Four mating systems are relevant in African production:

  • Hand mating: Ram is introduced to individually identified ewes in oestrus. Highest control, highest labour. Best for recording parentage and for targeted lambing.
  • Pen mating: Small group of ewes (10â15) with one ram for a defined period. Good balance of control and labour.
  • Pasture/group mating: Ram runs with the flock continuously. Lowest labour, lowest control, no parentage records.
  • Artificial insemination (AI): Increasingly available in South Africa, Kenya, Ethiopia and Nigeria. Allows use of superior genetics without owning a ram. Requires synchronisation and technical support.

Timing rule of thumb: the "AM/PM rule" â ewes detected in oestrus in the morning are mated that evening; ewes detected in the evening are mated the following morning. This places mating approximately 12â18 hours after onset, aligning with ovulation.

Flushing â increasing ewe nutrition (energy) 2â3 weeks before and during mating â can lift ovulation rate by 10â20% and is one of the cheapest interventions available. In practice, this means supplementing with 200â300 g of concentrate per ewe per day, or moving ewes to better pasture.

Table 2. Mating systems compared for African smallholder and commercial flocks
System Ram:ewe ratio Labour Parentage records Best for
Hand mating 1:1 (per session) High Yes Pedigree breeding, AI programmes
Pen mating 1:10â15 Medium Partial Small commercial flocks
Pasture/group mating 1:25â40 Low No Village/communal flocks
Artificial insemination n/a High (technical) Yes Genetic improvement programmes

Sources: ILRI (2013); FAO (2012); South African Small Stock Association extension materials (2021).

4. Pregnancy Management

Gestation in sheep averages 147 days (range 145â152). Pregnancy diagnosis is possible from day 35â40 using ultrasound, or from day 60â70 by experienced palpation. In the African context, where ultrasound is often unavailable, body condition monitoring and observation of oestrus return (a ewe that returns to heat 17â21 days after mating is not pregnant) are practical alternatives.

Nutrition is the single biggest determinant of pregnancy outcome. The last 6 weeks of gestation (when 70% of foetal growth occurs) is when underfeeding causes low birth weights, weak lambs and pregnancy toxaemia. Ewes carrying twins need 20â30% more energy than singles. In practice, this means supplementing with 300â500 g of concentrate per ewe per day in late gestation, plus good-quality forage.

Vaccination timing matters: clostridial vaccines (e.g., pulpy kidney, tetanus) should be given 4â6 weeks before lambing so that antibodies pass into colostrum. Deworming should be done at mating and again 4 weeks before lambing, using a product safe for pregnant ewes.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Pregnancy Toxaemia (Ketosis)

Pregnancy toxaemia is a life-threatening metabolic emergency in ewes carrying twins/triplets, especially in the last 6 weeks of gestation. Signs: off-feed, dull, staggering, sweet/acetone breath, lying down. Act immediately: call a veterinarian, drench with glucose or propylene glycol (60â100 ml twice daily), and offer palatable feed. Untreated cases die within 2â4 days. Prevention is cheaper than cure â never let late-gestation ewes lose body condition. This is the most common avoidable cause of ewe death in African smallholder flocks.

5. Lambing and Assistance

Normal lambing takes 30â120 minutes per lamb. The ewe should be observed quietly from a distance. Intervene only if: no progress after 1 hour of active straining, malpresentation (head back, legs back, breech), or if the ewe is exhausted.

When assisting: wash hands, use lubricant, correct the presentation, and pull only during the ewe's contractions, using gentle traction in a downward arc. Never pull with force â this causes vaginal tears and lamb death. After delivery, clear the lamb's mouth and nose, and ensure it breathes. Dip the navel in iodine (2â7%) to prevent joint ill and navel ill.

For African producers, the most common lambing problems are: (1) malnutrition-induced weak contractions, (2) malpresentation in single large lambs from overfed ewes, and (3) lack of clean, dry birthing areas leading to infection.

6. Neonatal Care

The first 24 hours determine whether a lamb survives. Colostrum â the first milk, rich in antibodies â must be consumed within 6 hours of birth, ideally within 1â2 hours. Lambs that do not receive adequate colostrum are 5â10Ã more likely to die in the first month. For orphaned or rejected lambs, use frozen/thawed colostrum from another ewe, or a commercial colostrum replacer.

Practical neonatal checklist: ensure the lamb is dry, warm, and has suckled; identify and record the lamb (ear tag or paint mark); ensure the ewe has passed the placenta within 6 hours; provide clean water and hay to the ewe; and observe for mastitis or metritis.

Lamb mortality in African smallholder flocks often runs 15â30%, but well-managed flocks can hold it below 8%. The difference is almost entirely management: colostrum, hygiene, shelter and nutrition.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Condition score ewes and rams 3 weeks before mating. Target BCS 2.5â3.5. Flush ewes with 200â300 g concentrate/day.
  2. Use the AM/PM rule. Ewe in heat AM â mate PM; ewe in heat PM â mate next AM.
  3. Keep ram:ewe ratios correct. 1:25â40 for pasture mating; 1:10â15 for pen mating; never overwork a ram.
  4. Vaccinate ewes 4â6 weeks pre-lambing (clostridial vaccine) and deworm 4 weeks pre-lambing.
  5. Boost late-gestation nutrition. 300â500 g concentrate/day in the last 6 weeks; twins need more.
  6. Watch for pregnancy toxaemia. Off-feed, dull, acetone breath in late gestation = emergency. Call vet, drench glucose.
  7. Ensure colostrum within 6 hours of birth. Dip navel in iodine. Record lamb and dam.
  8. Keep records. Mating date, sire, lambing date, lambs born/alive/weaned. Records turn breeding into a business.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Phenotypic Characterization of Animal Genetic Resources (2012) â free PDF, covers breeding and selection in African contexts.
  • ILRI â Sheep and Goat Production Handbook for Ethiopia â practical, free, Africa-specific.
  • MLA â Making More From Sheep (Australia) â free modules adaptable to African conditions.
  • WOAH â Terrestrial Animal Health Code â free, official animal health and welfare standards.
  • FAO â Small Ruminant Production Manual â free, covers reproduction, nutrition and health.

Business note: Breeding is not a cost centre â it is the engine of flock productivity. Every improvement in lambing rate, lamb survival and weaning weight compounds across the flock. Record your numbers, compare them to the benchmarks in this lesson, and make one improvement per season. That is how African sheep enterprises move from subsistence to sustainable profit.

quiz.q: How long is the estrous cycle of a ewe?
quiz.explanation: The average estrous cycle is 17 days, with a range of 14â19 days.

quiz.q: What is the gestation period of a sheep?
quiz.explanation: Sheep pregnancy lasts about 147 days (5 months).

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of heat in a ewe?
options: A) Standing still when the ram nudges her
quiz.explanation: A ewe in heat will stand to be mounted and may wag her tail.

quiz.q: What is a teaser ram?
options: A) A ram that is too old to breed
B) A vasectomized ram used to detect heat
C) A ram with a marking harness
D) A ram that is aggressive
quiz.explanation: A teaser ram cannot impregnate but will mount ewes in heat, helping you identify them.

quiz.q: How many ewes can a healthy mature ram serve in a 6-week pasture mating period?
quiz.explanation: A mature ram can serve 30â50 ewes in a 6-week period if in good condition.

quiz.q: What is flushing in sheep breeding?
options: A) Giving extra feed before mating to increase ovulation
B) Washing the ram before mating
quiz.explanation: Flushing means feeding ewes extra grain 2â3 weeks before mating to boost ovulation and twins.

quiz.q: Which body condition score is ideal for a breeding ram?
quiz.explanation: A ram should be in condition score 3â4 (on a 1â5 scale) to mate well.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid inbreeding?
options: A) It makes sheep grow faster
B) It causes small, weak lambs and lower fertility
quiz.explanation: Inbreeding leads to reduced vigour, smaller lambs, and fertility problems.

quiz.q: What is the best age range for a breeding ewe?
quiz.explanation: Ewes between 2 and 6 years old are most productive and have fewer problems.

quiz.q: How long should you quarantine a new ram before mixing with your flock?
quiz.explanation: A 3-week quarantine helps prevent bringing diseases into your flock.

quiz.q: In hand mating, how often should you check ewes for heat?
quiz.explanation: Checking morning and evening helps catch ewes in heat for timely mating.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a marking harness on a ram?
options: A) To protect the ram's chest
B) To identify which ewes have been mated
C) To make the ram more attractive
D) To measure the ram's weight
quiz.explanation: The crayon marks ewes during mating, so you know which ones were served.

quiz.q: When is the best time to mate ewes in many African regions?
options: B) So lambs are born when grass is plentiful
quiz.explanation: Mating should be timed so lambing coincides with good pasture to support milk production.

quiz.q: What percentage of lamb weight is gained in the last 2 months of pregnancy?
quiz.explanation: About 70% of fetal growth occurs in the last 6 weeks of pregnancy.

quiz.q: Which mineral deficiency can cause problems in pregnant ewes in some African soils?
quiz.explanation: Selenium and copper deficiencies are common in parts of Africa and can affect reproduction.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid feeding mouldy hay to pregnant ewes?
quiz.explanation: Mouldy feed can contain mycotoxins that cause abortion.

quiz.q: How long should second-stage labour (pushing) normally take?
quiz.explanation: If a ewe pushes hard for over an hour with no lamb, you should assist.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to pull a lamb during assistance?
options: A) Pull upwards towards the ewe's back
B) Pull downwards towards the ewe's hocks
quiz.explanation: Pulling downwards and backwards during a contraction matches the natural birth curve.

quiz.q: What should you dip the lamb's navel in after birth?
quiz.explanation: Iodine (7% tincture) disinfects the navel and prevents infection.

quiz.q: How soon should a newborn lamb suckle colostrum?
quiz.explanation: Colostrum must be consumed within the first hour for best antibody absorption.

quiz.q: What is colostrum?
options: A) The first milk, rich in antibodies
quiz.explanation: Colostrum is the thick, yellow first milk that provides immunity to the lamb.

quiz.q: How much colostrum should a lamb get in the first 6 hours?
quiz.explanation: A lamb needs at least 200 ml of colostrum in the first 6 hours of life.

quiz.q: What is a common cause of lamb scours?
quiz.explanation: Scours (diarrhoea) is often caused by dirty, wet pens and poor hygiene.

quiz.q: What is a creep feed?
options: B) A small pen with feed only for lambs
quiz.explanation: A creep feed area allows lambs to eat solid food without competition from adults.

quiz.q: At what age should lambs be vaccinated against clostridial diseases?
quiz.explanation: Lambs are typically vaccinated at 6â8 weeks of age.

quiz.q: What is the ideal birth weight for a lamb?
quiz.explanation: A healthy lamb weighs between 2 and 4 kg at birth, depending on breed.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of a ewe about to lamb?
quiz.explanation: Ewes often isolate themselves and paw the ground before lambing.

quiz.q: What should you do if a ewe has a retained placenta for over 6 hours?
quiz.explanation: Retained placenta can cause infection; a vet may need to treat with antibiotics or hormones.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record mating dates?
options: B) To know the ram's age
quiz.explanation: Knowing the mating date lets you calculate the expected lambing date (147 days later).

quiz.q: What is the best way to thaw frozen colostrum?
options: B) Thaw gently in warm water
quiz.explanation: Gentle thawing in warm water preserves antibodies; high heat destroys them.
